item.title: BadUSB Case
item.description:
BadUSB Case

The workstation collection contains three .lockd files, a ransom notice, a replacement background, a process-creation export, and a manifest. The USB image contains the program that sealed the files, but its staging directory is absent from the normal directory listing. Recovering that program is only half the job: a TLS callback changes its cipher constants before main, so a direct translation of the constants visible on disk produces the wrong key.

item.title: Verdict Engine
item.description:
Verdict Engine

The handout contains a Linux x86-64 executable, bpfgate, and its compiled rule file, rules/ingress.bpf. The executable reads one token from stdin. Exactly one printable, 32-byte token passes the shipped ruleset; that token is the flag.

Download bpfgate · Download ingress.bpf · Download solve.py

This solve reverses the rule program. It does not patch the executable or change the verdict path. The recovered token was submitted to the unmodified bpfgate and produced verdict: PASS.

item.title: A Matter of Time
item.description:
A Matter of Time

This crackme builds its AES key from a Windows account name. Its IV depends on a file timestamp and the executable’s PE timestamp. The code is split across jump trampolines and duplicated blocks, which makes the first decompiler output misleading.

The useful break was CBC itself: the IV affects only the first plaintext block. Once the right username decrypted the remaining blocks, I could work on the first block separately.

item.title: Connected
item.description:
Connected

Download solver

The handout is a Linux executable with C++ source in connected/source_code. The README also discloses the intended packet path and final flag. The useful reversing exercise is to explain why one particular message reaches PC1, then replay it against the unmodified executable. No outside host is contacted: the PCs, switches, and routers are simulated inside the process.

1. Follow the input through the simulated network

src/main.cpp prompts for what and where. The target address is 100.25.26.10. It accepts a packet from the user only when the message starts with msg_, then strips those four bytes. Sending directly to PC1 does not work because PC1’s handler rejects a packet whose sender is the user.

item.title: cryptpad
item.description:
cryptpad

Download solver

The handout contains a small Windows text editor and an encrypted file. The editor generates a random RC4 key for each saved file, then appends the key to that same file. Recovering the flag therefore requires understanding the file layout, not brute-forcing RC4.

CMO{r0ll_y0ur_0wn_b4d_c0d3}

The Python implementation below agrees with the original x86 decryption routine executed in Unicorn. This solve does not require starting the GUI or contacting a service.

item.title: Fatmike 02 — Record Player
item.description:
Fatmike 02 — Record Player

Download solver

The record player forces backward playback and pitch processing when the PLAY button is pressed. The official solution describes changing those two settings. I reproduced the patches against the handout and extracted the flag directly from its audio resource, then checked the result with the original hash function.

CMO{y0u_g0t_r1ckr0ll3d}

The verification here is offline: original x64 code confirms the hash and the effect of the two patches. I did not launch the complete GUI or listen to playback.

item.title: FlipVM
item.description:
FlipVM

Download solver

The handout contains a Linux x86-64 VM (FlipVM) and its signed bytecode (code.flp). The public repository also includes VM/compiler source and an official patch script. I ran that patch against the exact distributed bytecode and executed the patched program in the unmodified native VM. The valid input and flag are disclosed in the repository; the replay demonstrates the path through the distributed VM.

1. Check whether the prompt accepts input

Source_Code/Compiler/flipvmcode.ptf prints a prompt, then executes SLEEP 0, 500000000. Its development MOV R0, <expected input> instruction is commented out. It never reads stdin before hashing R0. An ordinary password typed at the prompt therefore cannot reach the comparison. This is visible in the source and confirmed by a normal handout run that displayed the banner and then the input-error branch.

item.title: FLRSCRNSVR
item.description:
FLRSCRNSVR

Download solver

The handout is a Windows screensaver executable in FLRSCRNSVR/handout/FLRSCRNSVR.zip; the archive password is flare. The repository includes its official solution, which identifies the registry value and encoding routine. I reproduced the inverse transformation against the encrypted table in the binary. This is an offline reconstruction, not a GUI acceptance test.

1. Locate the input and comparison

The screensaver’s configuration path (/c) reads Text under HKCU\Software\FLRSCRNSVR. It requires 25 characters and transforms them before comparing the result to a 25-entry, little-endian UTF-16 table. The screensaver and preview paths (/s, /p) are display modes; they are not needed to recover the text.

item.title: httpd
item.description:
HTTPD

Download solver

The executable looks like a small HTTP server, but the flag does not come from a URL. A background packet-capture routine watches ICMP traffic, extracts selected bytes, and uses them as an AES key and IV.

Recovered flag:

CMO{fUn_w1th_m4g1c_p4ck3t5}

This solve reproduces the packet checks and AES calculation offline using the supplied source and ciphertext extracted from the binary. The FreeBSD executable was not run under Linux, and no packets were sent to a live host.

item.title: Matryoshka v2
item.description:
Matryoshka v2

Download solver · Recovered license keys

This challenge puts one Windows DLL inside another. Each outer DLL checks the next 32 bytes of a license, uses those bytes as an RC4 key, decrypts a DLL resource, and calls the new DLL with the remaining license. The large file is mostly encrypted inner layers, not one giant validation function.

The solution below recovers the keys from the validation code and checks them against the original shellcode before decrypting each resource. It does not patch the license checker to accept an arbitrary key: that would leave RC4 using the wrong bytes and produce an invalid inner image.

item.title: What Did You Type
item.description:
What Did You Type

Download solver

The archive contains two PCAPs: one records USB keyboard traffic, and the other records files being uploaded over HTTP. The supplied PbWE.txt is a Base64-encoded encrypted ZIP containing the program responsible for the upload.

The recovered flag is:

CMO{Dumb357_P3r50n_1n_7h3_M1lky_W4y_!!!}

It is split between an XLSX cell, handwriting in a JPG, and a DOCX watermark. All three files were recovered from the network capture. The JPG fragment was read visually; the solver labels that transcription rather than pretending to perform OCR. The result also matches the repository author’s published flag.
